title: What is one customer worth?
principle: A customer is worth the margin on all their future buys.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a famous study from 1990. Two researchers, Frederick Reichheld and Earl Sasser, studied service businesses such as banks. They asked one question: what happens to profit when a few more customers stay?

screens.prompt: Imagine a business keeps 5 more customers out of every 100 each year. What do you think happens to its profit?
screens.why: They estimated profits could rise by 25% to 85%, depending on the business. Keeping 5 more customers out of 100 may seem small. But customers who stay keep buying year after year.

screens.title: Customer lifetime value
screens.text: The money you keep from one customer over the years is called customer lifetime value, or LTV. Count the margin you keep, not the full price. To find LTV, multiply the margin on each order × orders a year × years they stay.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: The studies looked at banks, but the same idea works for your bakery. It's June. One family has ordered from you for three years. They buy four birthday cakes every year. You keep ₹450 from each ₹850 cake.

screens.prompt: A family orders 4 cakes a year. You keep ₹450 per cake. If they stay 5 more years, how much will you keep?
screens.why: Yes. ₹450 × 4 cakes = ₹1,800 a year. Over 5 years, that makes ₹9,000. Don't think of this family as just one ₹850 order. You could earn ₹9,000 from them if they keep buying.

wrong.a: ₹1,800 is one year: ₹450 × 4. They stay 5 years, so ₹1,800 × 5 = ₹9,000.
wrong.c: You used the full price: ₹850 × 4 × 5. Lifetime value counts what you keep: ₹450 × 4 × 5 = ₹9,000.

screens.text: The café deal leaves you ₹1,750 a week. Over 50 weeks: ₹1,750 × 50 = ___ a year, and 2 years make ___.
screens.why: Yes. ₹1,750 × 50 = ₹87,500 a year. Over 2 years, that makes ₹1,75,000. The café brings you much more than one order. It's your biggest customer.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six ideas. For each one, tell me: will it increase lifetime value, or only help you sell today?

items.text: Send a message a week before each child's birthday
Give anyone ₹100 off this Sunday only
Remember each family's favourite cake flavour
Give a bigger cake at the same price, just once
Write down each family's birthdays and past orders
Put a festival sale banner on your menu

screens.why: Good. The first group helps families stay and order again. You remind them, remember their favourite flavour and know their birthdays. The second group helps you make one sale but may not bring them back.

screens.prompt: You want to offer a ₹400 trial cake to new families. You earn nothing from it. When is this a good idea?

options.label: When many families place first orders
When other bakers charge lower prices

screens.why: Yes. Remember Unit 3: a cheap first offer works only if buyers return and pay full price. You earn nothing from the trial cake. You earn money when the family comes back.

wrong.b: Many orders that earn ₹0 still leave you ₹0. Remember Unit 3: a cheap first offer works only if buyers return and pay full price.
wrong.c: Then you would be trying to beat other bakers on price. Remember Unit 3: a cheap first offer works only if buyers return and pay the full ₹850.

screens.setup: It's mid-June, 3 pm. A family that orders 4 cakes a year calls. Their birthday cake arrived crushed. Making a new one costs ₹400 and takes two hours. The party starts at 7 pm.
screens.question: What do you do?

options.label: Say sorry and offer ₹100 off the next cake
options.outcome: They still have a crushed cake for tonight's party. They thank you, but they are unhappy. Next birthday, they order from someone else. You saved ₹400 but lost about ₹9,000 over the next five years.
options.why: You saved ₹400 today but lost a family worth about ₹9,000.
options.better: Make a new cake now and deliver it free before 7 pm.

options.label: Make a new cake and deliver it for free
options.outcome: The new cake arrives at 6:30 pm. The mother shares a photo of the candles and thanks you in the colony group. They keep ordering. You spent ₹400 to keep a family worth about ₹9,000.
options.why: You compared the ₹400 cost with what the family could earn you over the years, not just one cake.

options.label: Give back the full ₹850 and say sorry
options.outcome: They're happy to get their money back, but they must buy a cake from a shop for tonight. Next time, they're not sure they can trust you. You lost ₹850 and may lose the family.
options.why: Giving the money back was fair. But they needed a cake for the party, and you did not give them one.
options.better: Make a new cake now and deliver it free before 7 pm.

screens.text: A customer is worth the ___ from all their ___ orders, not just the first.
screens.why: Yes. Reichheld and Sasser estimated that keeping a few more customers could increase profits a lot. The family whose cake was crushed is worth about ₹9,000, not just ₹850.

summary: Customer lifetime value (LTV): the total margin you keep from one customer over the years.
LTV = margin per order × orders per year × years they stay.
When a customer has a problem, compare the cost of fixing it with their lifetime value, not just one order.

cards.front: A family buys 4 cakes a year. You keep ₹450 per cake for 5 years. What is their LTV?
Which amount from each order do you use to find lifetime value?
cards.back: Count the margin you keep, not the full price.

cards.front: Fixing a regular customer's problem costs ₹400. Their lifetime value is ₹9,000. Should you fix it?
cards.back: Compare the cost of fixing the problem with the customer's lifetime value.

sources.label: Reichheld and Sasser, Zero Defections: Quality Comes to Services (Harvard Business Review, Sep–Oct 1990)
Ipsos, Shattering myths about customer loyalty (quotes the 25% to 85% finding)
Reichheld, Here's the truth about customer retention (American Banker, 1991)
